title: Authenticated RCE via eval() of workflow custom transform expression
description: The workflow execution engine evaluates attacker-supplied transform expressions with JavaScript eval() without any sanitization or sandboxing. An authenticated user with ordinary 'member' role in an organization can supply a workflow whose action node carries a crafted custom transform expression, execute it, and achieve arbitrary code execution in the backend Node.js process.
impact: Full server-side code execution in the backend process: arbitrary file read/write (demonstrated by writing a marker file via fs.writeFileSync), access to the entire process environment (demonstrated by enumerating process.env), and by extension the Postgres/Redis/S3/AWS credentials held by the process. This compromises all tenants' data.
technical_analysis:
`POST /workflows/:workflowId/execute` (backend/src/routes/execution.routes.ts:154) is guarded by `authenticate, requireModifyAccess, enforceTokenQuota`. `requireModifyAccess = requireRole('owner','admin','member')` (backend/src/middleware/auth.ts:280), so any ordinary org member qualifies. The request body's `canvasData.nodes` is validated only as `z.array(z.unknown())` (backend/src/schemas/workflow.schema.ts:48), so node content — including transform configurations — is fully attacker-controlled. During execution the action executor dispatches to `applyCustomTransform` (backend/src/services/node-executors/action-executor.ts:195), which at lines 316-325 substitutes the `data` placeholder and calls `eval(evalExpr)` with the raw attacker-supplied `transformConfig.expression`. There is no allowlist, sandbox, or vm isolation; the code's own comment in the sibling code-artifact executor acknowledges "In production, use vm2 or isolated-vm".

Scope note on the same class: `applyFilter`/`applyReduce` (lines 265, 290) contain equivalent eval sinks but are unreachable from the dispatch switch. The condition-executor's eval is neutralized by a paren-blocking regex. `code-artifact-executor.ts:296` (`const result = eval(code)`) is a second live sink of the same class, currently blocked only incidentally: a top-level `return` in the generated code throws a SyntaxError before eval. Fixing that functional bug without replacing eval re-opens it; any fix must cover both sinks.
poc_description:
1. Authenticate as any user who is a 'member' (or higher) of an organization.
2. Create or edit a workflow whose canvasData contains an action node with a transform config of type 'custom' whose expression is crafted JavaScript.
3. POST /api/workflows/:workflowId/execute with the crafted canvasData.
4. The engine reaches applyCustomTransform, which evals the expression in-process.
5. Observe side effects: a marker file written to disk via process.getBuiltinModule('fs').writeFileSync, and Object.keys(process.env).length returned through the node output — arbitrary code execution confirmed.
remediation_steps: Remove eval from the transform pipeline. Replace expression evaluation with a restricted, whitelisted transformation DSL or a sandboxed interpreter (e.g. isolated-vm with no host bindings), and validate transform expressions server-side before persisting or executing them. Apply the same treatment to code-artifact-executor.ts:296, which evals node 'code' fields of the same provenance. Ensure workflow canvas node payloads are structurally validated (schema-restricted), not z.array(z.unknown()).
evidence: PoC ran locally against the real backend module (vitest, node_modules pre-existing, S3/DB mocked): the crafted expression using process.getBuiltinModule('fs').writeFileSync created the marker file on disk, and Object.keys(process.env).length executed with its value returned in the node output — arbitrary code execution confirmed on the vulnerable code path.
assumptions: Assumes the workflow execute route is exposed to authenticated tenant users in production (role 'member' is included in requireModifyAccess). Local runtime validation used the real backend code with mocked AWS dependencies; production deployment exposure is unverified.
counterevidence: Searched for sanitization/containment on the path: nodes are validated only as z.array(z.unknown()) (workflow.schema.ts), and the preHandlers on the execute route are authenticate, requireModifyAccess, enforceTokenQuota — no content filter on node expressions. eval executes in-process, so no vm2/isolated-vm sandbox applies. The only mitigations found are that the attacker must be an authenticated org member with modify access to the workflow, and that sibling paths (applyFilter/applyReduce) happen to be unreachable. No WAF or expression allowlist exists in the code path examined.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that the workflow execute endpoint is reachable by unauthenticated or self-service-registered users in production would raise severity toward critical; conversely, evidence that transform expressions are filtered by an upstream allowlist not present in this repository would lower it.

title: Unauthenticated WebSocket subscription to arbitrary execution events at /ws/executions
description: The /ws/executions WebSocket endpoint registers with no authentication preHandler and performs no ownership or tenant check on subscription. Any unauthenticated client that can reach the API can subscribe to arbitrary workflow executions and receive execution events, breaking tenant isolation of execution streams.
impact: Unauthenticated cross-tenant subscription to execution event streams. The subscription to an arbitrary executionId was confirmed; events may carry node outputs, errors, and intermediate results (verified only as subscription success and event routing — the sensitivity of the data carried in event payloads in production was not exhaustively enumerated). Potential availability impact from unauthenticated connection flooding. No integrity impact demonstrated.
technical_analysis: In backend/src/websocket/execution.gateway.ts:135-141, the route `fastify.get('/ws/executions', { websocket: true }, handler)` is registered with no `preHandler` — unlike sibling HTTP routes which use `authenticate`. `handleConnection` accepts the socket without verifying the request's JWT or tenant. `handleSubscribe` (line 232) validates only that `executionId` is a non-empty string (lines 233-242); there is no lookup of the execution record, no ownership check, and no tenant comparison, after which the client is added to that execution's subscriber set. Because the execution ID space is UUIDs, guessing an active ID is low probability per attempt, but any leaked/reconnoitered executionId grants live event access, and the endpoint additionally allows unauthenticated connection resource consumption.
poc_description:
1. With no credentials or session, open a WebSocket to ws(s)://<host>/ws/executions.
2. Send {"type":"subscribe","executionId":"<any UUID>"}.
3. Receive {"type":"subscribed"} — the client is now registered on that execution's broadcast list and receives all subsequent events for it.
remediation_steps: Require authentication on the /ws/executions route (verify the Cognito JWT during the WebSocket handshake, e.g. via the preHandler or the verifyClient/upgrade path) and, in handleSubscribe, verify that the authenticated user's organization/tenant owns the requested executionId (load the execution record and compare tenant) before adding the client to the subscribers map.
evidence: Local runtime PoC against the real gateway module (S3/DB mocked): an unauthenticated ws client connected to /ws/executions, sent {"type":"subscribe","executionId":"<arbitrary-uuid>"}, and received {"type":"subscribed"} confirming the subscription to another tenant's execution stream.
assumptions: Assumes the WebSocket gateway is mounted on the public API in production (same registration path as HTTP routes). Production exposure and whether events carry sensitive node outputs at scale are unverified.
counterevidence: Checked the route registration (no preHandler array, unlike HTTP routes which use [authenticate, requireModifyAccess, ...]) and the full handleSubscribe path — no tenant/ownership verification exists anywhere between connection and subscription confirmation. The 'subscribed' confirmation and routing to broadcast were verified at runtime; what the event payload contains beyond the verified subscription flow was not exhaustively enumerated, and that uncertainty is reflected in a Medium confidentiality rating.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that execution event payloads include node outputs or other tenant-sensitive content in production would raise confidentiality and severity; evidence that the gateway is only bound to an authenticated internal network in deployment would lower it.

title: Path traversal in agentcore workspace-sync S3 restore and related workspace-manager path containment weaknesses
description: Three related path-containment weaknesses in the agentcore workspace layer allow filesystem paths to escape their intended directory when untrusted path components are joined without canonical containment checks. The primary instance is the agentcore workspace-sync S3 restore routine; two sibling weaknesses in the backend workspace-manager share the same root-cause family (missing or incorrect path containment).
impact: Primary: with attacker-controlled S3 keys under the workspace prefix, arbitrary file write (overwrite) anywhere the process can write, including host config, application files, or other tenants' workspace directories. Sibling (a): cross-session file access within the same org/scope when a session ID is a prefix of another. Sibling (b): unvalidated filePath permits cross-tenant S3 reads if any session-scoped path is reachable. Scope is limited by the stated prerequisites of each instance.
technical_analysis:
**Primary — agentcore/src/workspace-sync.ts:77-85 (sink at line 94).** On restore, `relativePath = key.slice(prefix.length)` then `localPath = path.join(WORKSPACE_DIR, relativePath)` with no containment check before `fs.mkdirSync`/write. S3 keys containing `../` segments resolve outside `/workspace`. Prerequisite: attacker-controlled keys under the workspace prefix (e.g. a shared or compromised bucket) — no tenant-reachable write primitive into this prefix was found in this codebase. The path arithmetic was validated locally with mocked S3 and the real `path.join`/fs behavior; no control exists between the join and the write.

**Sibling (a) — backend/src/services/workspace-manager.ts:1547-1555 (resolveWorkspaceFilePath).** `resolved.startsWith(workspacePath)` without a trailing separator: a path like `../sessionA-evil/...` passes the check when the current session ID is a prefix of another (`sessionA` vs `sessionA-evil`), enabling cross-session file access within the same org/scope. The bypass was verified against the real implementation.

**Sibling (b) — backend/src/services/workspace-manager.ts:1495-1530 (readWorkspaceFileFromS3).** The `filePath` parameter is interpolated directly into the S3 key `${orgId}/${scopeId}/${sessionId}/${filePath}` without validation, so `../` segments (or leading `/`) can target keys outside the session prefix on read. Reachability depends on its callers; no validated caller chain to an attacker-controlled `filePath` was demonstrated, so it is recorded as a related weakness, not a standalone confirmed exploit.

All three share one root cause: untrusted path components joined without canonical containment verification.
poc_description:
1. Mock the S3 ListObjectsV2 result to include a key of the form <prefix>../../etc/poc_marker.
2. Run the workspace-sync restore routine.
3. Observe localPath resolves outside /workspace and the marker file is written at the escaped location (confirmed by real path.join arithmetic; no named containment control exists).
remediation_steps: After every join with an untrusted path component, canonicalize the result (path.resolve) and verify containment with a separator-aware check (e.g. resolved === root || resolved.startsWith(root + path.sep)). In workspace-sync, reject any key whose sliced relative path begins with '..', resolves to an absolute path, or escapes WORKSPACE_DIR. Apply the separator-aware fix to resolveWorkspaceFilePath, and apply the same canonical containment validation to the filePath used to build S3 keys in readWorkspaceFileFromS3 / readWorkspaceFileFromS3Raw.
evidence: Local PoC (mocked S3 listing, real fs/path code): a workspace-sync key of the form <prefix>../../etc/poc_marker produced localPath /etc/poc_marker — the escape succeeds in real path arithmetic. For the sibling: with workspacePath ending in 'sessionA' (no separator), startsWith('sessionA-evil/...') resolves to true, bypassing the containment check in resolveWorkspaceFilePath.
assumptions: Primary vector (S3 key control) requires the attacker to control object keys under the workspace prefix — no tenant-reachable write primitive into that prefix was found, so it presupposes a shared or compromised bucket scenario. Sibling weaknesses operate through the session/workspace API with authenticated session access. Local validation used mocked S3 against real filesystem/SDK code.
counterevidence: Traced the primary vector's prerequisites: workspace-sync reads keys from a ListObjectsV2 on a configured prefix, and no tenant-reachable API writes arbitrary keys into that prefix — the write primitive itself is the missing link, making this a shared/compromised-bucket scenario rather than a directly exploitable tenant path. The resolveWorkspaceFilePath check exists and does enforce containment except for the separator defect; readWorkspaceFileFromS3 callers were inspected but the tenant-facing chain for it was not fully traced to a live route. These constraints are stated rather than used to dismiss the finding.
confidence_rationale: The path-escape mechanics were validated with real fs operations and mocked S3, and the missing containment checks were confirmed by direct code reading at the cited lines. However, the primary S3-key vector lacks a demonstrated attacker-controlled write path in this codebase, and production reachability of each sibling's caller chain is unverified.
severity_change_conditions: Discovery of a tenant-reachable primitive that writes attacker-controlled keys into the workspace S3 prefix would raise this to high/critical; confirmation that the workspace bucket is never shared across trust domains and session IDs cannot prefix one another would lower it.

title: Unrestricted server-side fetch (SSRF) with response readback in workflow API-call node
description: The workflow API-call node executes server-side fetches to fully attacker-controlled URLs with no allowlist, private-IP, or scheme restriction. Any authenticated organization member (the lowest privilege role) can point a workflow node at internal targets such as the cloud instance metadata service (169.254.169.254), loopback services, or RFC1910 hosts, set arbitrary request headers, and read the full response body back through the execution result.
impact: An authenticated low-privilege org member can exfiltrate the application server's cloud instance metadata credentials (AWS IMDS, GCP/Azure equivalents reachable from the host), probe and read internal services (Redis admin, admin panels, Kubernetes endpoints), and pivot those credentials into the cloud account. Demonstrated: arbitrary internal URL + attacker-chosen method/headers + complete response body returned to the caller via the workflow execution result.
technical_analysis: `executeApiCall` in `src/services/node-executors/action-executor.ts` takes `apiConfig` from the workflow node's `data.metadata` (line 98-100), substitutes workflow variables into the URL (line 103: `this.substituteVariables(apiConfig.url, context)`) and into headers (line 111-114), then performs `fetch(url, { method: apiConfig.method || 'GET', headers: {...attacker headers}, ... })` at line 123 with no URL validation of any kind — no allowlist, no scheme restriction, no private/internal IP filtering. The response body is parsed and returned in the node result (`response`/`result` fields, lines 143-152), and on failure the raw response body is included in the error, so the response is readable either way. Reachability: workflow definitions and their nodes are persisted user content; the execution route `POST /api/workflows/:workflowId/execute` (src/routes/execution.routes.ts:154) requires only `authenticate, requireModifyAccess, enforceTokenQuota`, and `requireModifyAccess` is `requireRole('owner','admin','member')` (src/middleware/auth.ts:280) — i.e. every ordinary member of an organization. Sibling surface: the same unvalidated fetch exists for MCP server health-checks in `src/services/mcp.service.ts` (fetch of `config.url || server.host_address` with server-supplied headers) for org admins, giving a second path with limited readback (success/latency/status only). The skill-marketplace fetch sites (skill-marketplace.service.ts:184,315,605,624,647,661,683,696,731) are constrained to github.com/raw.githubusercontent.com/api.github.com via `parseGitHubUrl` (hostname !== 'github.com' → rejected) or fixed hostnames, and were ruled out.
poc_description: 1. As an authenticated org 'member', create a workflow containing an API-call action node whose apiConfig.url is an internal address (e.g. the instance metadata endpoint) and whose headers include any token the internal service expects. 2. Execute the workflow via the execute endpoint. 3. The node substitutes workflow variables into the URL, performs the server-side fetch with the attacker's headers, and places the full response body in the node result, which the caller reads from the execution output. Validated locally with a mocked global fetch asserting the URL, headers, and response readback.
remediation_steps: Restrict the API-call node's outbound requests: validate the resolved URL (after variable substitution, at execution time) against a denylist of non-routable ranges (loopback, RFC1910, link-local 169.254.0.0/16 including cloud metadata, IPv6 equivalents, and decimal/hex IP encodings), and optionally an allowlist of approved external hosts per organization. Enforce HTTPS-only unless explicitly opted in. Consider blocking or scrubbing user-settable headers that can bypass IMDSv2 protections. If arbitrary outbound HTTP is a deliberate product capability, gate it behind an explicit admin-configured egress policy rather than the default member role.
evidence: Local PoC (mocked global fetch — no network contact; scratch under /tmp/ssrfpoc) using the actual compiled ActionNodeExecutor: the fetch sink received `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/s3-role` after variable substitution of `{{env.role}}`, with the attacker-set header `X-aws-ec2-metadata-token`, and the node result carried the fetched body (`{"secret":"imds-role-credentials"}`) in `result.response`/`result.result`. Second assertion: `http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/health` reached the sink unvalidated. Both tests passed (vitest, 2/2). Source: node.data.metadata.apiConfig flows from the workflow definition authored by any 'member' via POST /api/workflows/:id/execute (execution.routes.ts:154).
assumptions: Requires an authenticated org member with workflow modify access (owner/admin/member — requireModifyAccess) who can create or edit a workflow with an API-call node. Deployment must place the backend on a network with reachable internal services (cloud metadata endpoint, internal admin panels), which is the normal deployment posture of this stack.
counterevidence: Checked for mitigations: no allowlist/denylist/private-IP guard anywhere on the path (action-executor.ts:100-160); execution route does require authentication plus requireModifyAccess, so anonymous exploitation is blocked; requireModifyAccess includes the ordinary 'member' role, so the privilege bar is low, not a control; a 30s default timeout exists but only bounds duration. The feature argument ("API-call node is intended to make arbitrary HTTP calls") is design intent, not a security control — the demonstrated ability of a low-privilege org member to reach link-local metadata and internal RFC1910 services with full readback is the exploitable consequence of shipping that feature with no network-scope restriction.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that the backend host's cloud metadata service is IMDSv2-only and its role has no permissions, or that the deployment network blocks egress to 169.254.169.254 and internal hosts, would reduce this to internal-network probing; conversely, proof that fetched credentials grant cloud resource access would raise it toward critical.
